column2: a merge does not certify the whole product.,proposed title route,"Five rounds of work on Zeus. Full handoff: `docs/ZEUS-PRIME-INTEGRATION.md`. Phase 0 reading of the repository: `docs/ZEUS-PRIME-INVENTORY.md`.

column1: State: **green, with four disclosed limits.** Not ""perfect"".
Zeus documented a great deal it could not actually do, and could not tell when a claim was a memory.
1. **Nothing Zeus learned reached a later turn.** `.zeus/eval-log.jsonl` was written by one script, read only by a stats printer, had no lesson field, and was empty.
2. **""Verified"" was a memory.** Nothing recorded which gate ran, at which round, against which version of the tree.
3. **""Implemented"" was a memory too.** Nothing held the work items, so a six-item request reported finished after four left no artifact saying so.
4. **The always-on core had no drift check.** Nothing proved the kernel stayed a faithful subset of the doctrine it compresses.

5. **7 of 39 Zeus scripts could be run by nothing** — no CLI verb, no package script, no hook, no CI step, no importer. Among them the entire delivery pipeline (`zeus-run-state.mjs`), the role planner, the merge guard and the release watcher.
6. **8 of 10 plainly-UI requests routed to no visual module**, so they got no visual requirements, no UI contract and no accessibility reviewer.
7. **Zeus never said what it thought a request meant**, so a misread surfaced only after the work.

**The reading, shown before the work.** Every actionable turn opens with how Zeus read the request, what it deliberately did *not* read it as, every inference it made, and the operator's words quoted back unedited — rendered before any classification field, because that is the line that catches a misread. It restates
column2: it never rewrites the request into different words and acts on those. Deterministic and offline: it runs in the hook on every prompt.

column1: **Plan ledger** (`pnpm zeus:plan`). The work items. An item is done only with a command and a zero exit code
column2: `close` refuses while any item is pending, active or blocked, and names each one. That refusal is the loop.

column1: **Spec compiler** (`zeus spec`). A request turned into something precise enough to implement: the routed modules' own requirement prose, the acceptance criteria, the owning role, the checks. It **never invents intent** — everything it cannot derive is a `TODO`, and `spec --check` refuses the file while one remains. For UI work it emits the twelve dimensions `zeus visual-contract` requires as questions, so a generated skeleton cannot satisfy that lint by shape alone.
**Gate ledger** (`pnpm zeus:gate`). Gate results bound to the workspace fingerprint `zeus-fingerprint.mjs` already computed. A failed gate is never skippable
column2: rounds are bounded by the tier's `repairRounds`
column3: `ship` refuses without the repository gate set and, where risk or radius requires review, **a passing review for every reviewer the changed paths call for** — not merely one. Where the paths resolve to no reviewer, a count applies instead: two independent reviews at high risk and above. Derived beats chosen: two reviews by the wrong two specialists satisfy a count and fail this.

column1: **Continual harness** (`pnpm zeus:harness`, proposed by `/zeus-refine`). Supplemental learned state with mandatory evidence, injected into every turn under a character budget, every mutation one rollback away within a 5-refinement window.

column1: 1. **No independent reviewer was dispatched.** This session was forbidden from using the Agent tool. Classifying Zeus's own surface changed this diff to **high risk, `production` blast radius**, and `pnpm zeus:gate ship` refuses it by name: `arq-architecture-reviewer`, `arq-release-reviewer` and `arq-security-ai-reviewer` have not passed. That refusal was left standing and red rather than satisfied with a recorded review that never happened. The merge proceeds on the repository owner's explicit instruction, with `engineering-gate` — which `CLAUDE.md` names as the actual merge authority, Zeus being advisory — green on the head commit. **Dispatching those three reviewers against the merged head remains outstanding work.**
2. **Every gate is self-attested.** Recording `typecheck --outcome pass` does not run `tsc`.

3. **`pnpm zeus:test` still does not run in CI**, because it asserts a p95 compile time under 20 ms that would flake on a shared runner. The drift guards, `zeus:validate` and the 147 Zeus tests do run.
4. **The reviewer match is only as good as the impact map.** An uncovered path yields `matched: false` and falls back to a count: fail-closed, but weaker than a match.

1. **Does the agent operating system deserve its own blast radius level?** `.zeus/`, `scripts/zeus-*` and `.claude/` are classified at `product` radius, which closes the fail-open. But `product` means ""user-visible product behaviour across packages"", and that is not what these files are. A seventh level would describe them honestly and would renumber a scale `zeus-validate.mjs` requires to be contiguous. That is a vocabulary decision.

2. **How much autonomy should the loop have?** The machinery that makes an autonomous loop safe is built — deterministic next-item, mandatory evidence, a refusal to close early. Unbounded self-continuation is deliberately not built.
3. **Should Arq have a Supabase backend at all?** There is none today.

column2: a merge does not certify the whole product.,proposed title route,"Three defects found by auditing the repository against its own evidence. Each is a case of a surface disagreeing with what the code does
column3: in every case the drift was possible because nothing was checking, so each fix ships with the check that would have caught it.

column1: | 1 | Public site says `.arq` projects cannot be opened. They can. | Claim promoted, conflict resolved, five pages corrected, six rendered tests |
| 2 | `NOTICE` says ARQ has no third-party code. It has 289 packages. | Rewritten, both reviewed exceptions named, bound to the SBOM by a new gate |
| 3 | Every reader downloads a PDF writer on first paint. | Deferred
column2: entry chunk −68% gzipped, with a budget and a browser check |

column1: **1. The open.** The site told readers that choosing an `.arq` file ends at a compatibility verdict and that opening it ""is not wired yet"". Three pages carried the denial, `native-arq-open` was `LIBRARY_ONLY`, and `DRIFT-NATIVE-OPEN-MARKETING` was an active **critical** conflict blocking the public, support and documentation surfaces.
That conflict is worth recording in the direction it actually ran. It was opened because copy promised an open the product could not perform
column2: it is closed because that same copy had become the opposite defect — denying an open the product had shipped. The registry caught the overclaim and then went on blocking a claim that had become true. A gate that only fails in the optimistic direction lets the product get quietly better than its own description, which is a nicer failure than lying and is still a failure. The 2026-08-11 marketing UI/UX pass (#309) reworked these very pages and did not catch it, because it audited presentation rather than truth.

column1: **2. The notices.** `NOTICE` — the attribution file `LICENSE` points at — said *""No third-party code has been incorporated into this repository yet - it currently contains planning documentation only""*, with a component table reading `(none yet)`. The build depends on 289 packages across 12 licence families, and `/legal/open-source` lists every one correctly from the same bill of materials the CI licence gate enforces. The repository was telling the truth to the public and the opposite to anyone reading its own legal file. The two packages it most needed to name were the ones missing: `web-ifc` (MPL-2.0) and `caniuse-lite` (CC-BY-4.0), the reviewed exceptions that carry obligations beyond attribution. `docs/product/DEPENDENCY-AND-LICENCE-POLICY.md` records the reasoning for both — the repository knew
column2: `NOTICE` was the only place that did not.

column1: **3. The bundle.** `App.tsx` imported the sheet exporter statically, so pdf-lib, fontkit and their font and encoding tables sat in the start-up chunk, reachable only by invoking the export command. The entry chunk was 1,761.63 kB raw / 743.02 kB gzipped. This is the second time it has been fixed: `4c31107` deferred the 3D surface and reached 614 kB / 193 kB, and it had since grown past the figure that prompted that work. The split was made once and nothing watched it.
Each fix is paired with the gate that makes it stick, because in all three cases an unenforced correction is what drifted.

- **Open**: claim → `CURRENT` (bounded to opening), conflict resolved with evidence, three bindings re-moded, two added for pages that now make a current-state claim. Copy corrected on home, product, architects and iPad, plus a dated changelog entry — the superseded 24 July entry points forward rather than being rewritten, since editing it would destroy the record of what was true when.
- **`DECISION-PERSISTENCE-TIERS`**: `unresolved-decision` → `evidence-insufficient`. Still blocking, but ADR-0028/0030 settled the architecture
column2: what is missing is a tested write flow. The two statuses ask for different work — one asks an owner for a decision already made, the other asks an engineer for a checkpoint path that does not exist.

column1: - **`NOTICE`**: states what is incorporated, names both exceptions with the obligation ARQ accepts, lists the licence families. It deliberately does not restate all 289 packages — a hand-maintained copy of generated data is exactly what went stale, and `NOTICE` already carried the instruction not to hand-edit it.
- **Bundle**: the exporter moves behind a dynamic import inside the export handler. 1,762 kB → 754 kB raw, 743 kB → 235 kB gzipped.
- No save or checkpoint path. Nothing writes back to the chosen `.arq` file, and no surface says otherwise
column2: `portable-arq-publication` stays `LIBRARY_ONLY`.

column1: - No claim about Safari on iPadOS. The open is measured in Chromium on a desktop runner, and the iPad page refuses to generalise from it.
- No licence-grant or repository-visibility decision. `LICENSE-DECISION-REQUIRED.md` records a verified conflict between the recorded decision and the observed repository state
column2: that is an owner decision with legal advice attached and this branch deliberately does not infer one.

column1: - No full STATUS.md reconciliation. Everything outside the claims section still dates from `0336cfa`, ~120 commits back, and now says so rather than presenting stale counts as current.
`benchmarks/results/native-open-capability.png` and `native-open-plan.png` re-recorded from this tree. The rendered home page was inspected directly at 1440px and 390px after the copy change.

Every guard here was checked by mutation — re-introducing the defect and confirming the guard fails — because a drift gate that silently stops matching recreates the exact failure it was written for, with a green tick over it.

- **Six rendered claim-binding tests**: each page bound to the open claim states the open, and states in the same place that the chosen file is not written to. Re-introducing the old denial and a fabricated save claim each failed the suite. One of those mutations then caught a later copy edit of my own that weakened the limit phrasing.

- **`check:notice-attribution`** (+ 15-case self-test): fails if `NOTICE` denies third-party code while the SBOM reports packages, if a licence family is unlisted, or if a non-blanket-allowed package is unnamed. Run against the original `NOTICE` it produces 14 findings. Includes the OR/AND asymmetry in licence expressions, where being wrong is silent both ways.

- **`check:web-bundle-budget`** (+ self-test): gzipped budget *and* marker-based absence of deferred libraries. Both are needed — a budget alone can be met while a split reverses. Reverting the dynamic import fires both.
- **`benchmark:sheet-export`**: drives the real command palette against the built bundle

Merged as a squash, `221c33b`, following this branch's `(#NNN)` convention. Rollback is therefore a single `git revert 221c33b`, not the three independent reverts this section described before the merge — corrected rather than left standing, because a rollback plan naming commits that no longer exist is worse than none.

Reverting is atomic by construction rather than by care. Claim state, conflict status and binding modes moved together and revert together, because the language verifiers reject any partial combination: a `current` binding on a non-`CURRENT` claim, or a `CURRENT` claim under an active conflict, each fail the gate. The bundle change reverts to a working, larger bundle, at which point `check:web-bundle-budget` fails — that is the intended signal, not a surprise. No data, schema or deployment state is involved.

To revert only part of it, the four pre-squash commits survive on the `claude/code-review-implementation-bnmp78` branch ref: `29faa2a` (claims and copy), `c7291a8` (`NOTICE`), `891a2c1` (bundle), `8b96d8e` (generated context refresh).
Two repository settings, both owner actions rather than code changes, and both the same shape as the defects fixed here — a gate correctly refusing to claim success on evidence it could not obtain.

**GitHub Pages is not enabled**, so the corrected copy is merged but not published. Discovered when this merge triggered the deploy: the `build` job passed, including the rendered-copy audit and the commit-bound deployment proof, and then `actions/deploy-pages` returned `404 … Ensure GitHub Pages has been enabled`. The same job failed identically on `d1e17a1` (#309) and `05424ac` (#308), so it predates this change by at least two PRs. `verify-live-language` was skipped in consequence, meaning no live site was checked either. Fix: Settings → Pages, then re-run the deploy workflow.

column1: **Content/copy-level fixes**: distinct `note--limit` visual role for limitation/caution text (4 pages) · home page reordered · security page splits ""observed behaviour"" from ""current architecture"" · interoperability format table gains a code-verified ""Library adapter"" column, fidelity legend expanded 8→11 governed terms · changelog restructured into a real timeline · contact page explains its no-external-links policy rather than fabricating clickable links that would violate a real, tested site-wide invariant · Privacy/Terms gained a document-status block · fixed a real CSS bug.

**Structural work** (the audit's largest item): the four page families (Story/Capability/Operational-truth/Reference) as a `family` field → class on `<main>` · Capability pages carry a ""NOW"" state marker in the brand accent answering ""can I do this today?"" in the first viewport · Reference pages lost their marketing CTA band · primary navigation regrouped from 7 flat items into Product/Solutions/Resources dropdowns + 2 direct links · footer's bordered title-block replaced with a quiet provenance strip.

**Four-level note-spacing hierarchy**: `notes()` supports an optional `separation: 'related' | 'chapter'` per entry, combined with the existing `kind` (limit/state) modifier. Measured on the built page: 32px (related) / 52px (default) / 96px + hairline rule (chapter). Applied to 6 transitions on home, security, product and changelog where uniform spacing was flattening real structural breaks.

**Comprehension-test rubric**: `docs/product/COMPREHENSION-TEST-RUBRIC.md` states, per page family, the one question a first-viewport read (hero + first note) should let a reader answer, then runs a grounded self-check quoting the actual rendered copy of all 17 pages against it. All 17 pass. It also caught `/interoperability` missing the `kind: 'state'` marker its four sibling capability pages carry, now fixed.
## Critical review of this branch's own work
A browser-evidence review pass over everything the branch changed, rather than re-reading the audit. It found **four real defects introduced by earlier commits here**, all now fixed and re-verified:

1. **Header typography split in two** (visual, every page). The nav regroup put group headings in `<summary>` elements, but the header's mono/uppercase typography was bound to `.site-nav a`, which never matches a summary. Measured: summaries rendered Plus Jakarta Sans 16px sentence-case beside direct links in JetBrains Mono 13px uppercase, in the same row — the header read as two navigation systems pushed together. Now computes identically for both.

2. **Open state signalled by colour alone** — open and ""you are in this section"" both tinted accent. The disclosure triangle now rotates when open (static transform, nothing for reduced-motion to suppress).

3. **`aria-label` on roles that prohibit it** (every page) — it sat on `

column1: The ARQ House 17.0 package recorded one open item for itself:
> The live ARQ application still needs to be tested opening and hydrating every Version 17 semantic element.
It was honest about it — its own validation carries `evidenceBoundary.productionARQWorkspaceHydrationVerified: false`.

Verifying it turned up something worse than a refusal. **The app accepted `house.arq` and silently gutted it.** `decodeNativeProjectModel` dispatches on a root `projectName`, and 17.0 carries one, so the app took the flat path — the shape this build writes for its own files — and adopted the project as **68 bare wall centrelines with `document: null`**. A user would have seen a stick drawing of their coordinated house and had no way to tell ""not drawn yet"" from ""thrown away"".

Fixing that exposed the larger version of the same fault. The model files **58 sections under `semanticExtensions`**, and no code in this repository had ever looked at any of them. 140 fixtures and furniture items, three floor plates, a two-flight dogleg stair, 126 services points, 188 room boundary lines — **387 items in total** — went in and never came out, uncounted. Arq was reading roughly a seventh of the file.
**1. Verified both artifacts.** All four published SHA-256s match
column2: ZIP integrity and the package's own 67-file checksum manifest pass with zero mismatches. Valid arqfs v2 container — `ARQ1`, `user_version` 2, `integrity_check` ok, no FK violations, all twelve tables.

column1: **2. `checkArqModelConformance`** enumerates every divergence in one pass instead of the reader's first-only, split by whether it blocks opening or is **silently lost**. That split found the dangerous one: 65 walls carry a bare `height` the reader does not read.

**3. `adaptArqHouse17Model`, wired into the app's decode path.** Every element hydrates: 3 levels, 5 wall types, 68 walls, 47 openings, 26 doors, 13 windows, 48 rooms. **Lossless three ways** — all 65 stated wall heights exact, every element id survives, no wall endpoint moves.

**4. `placed-content.ts`** reads the three `semanticExtensions` sections the model can carry today: **140 furnishings, 3 plates with their voids, 1 stair with 2 flights and 2 landings**, every level and room reference resolving. Rotation is resolved once, here, into world-space corners — a fifth of this fixture's items are turned, and two renderers each applying the angle themselves is how plan and 3D come to disagree about where a thing is.

Stairs are kept as flights and landings rather than as `bim-core`'s `StairInstance`, which is deliberately bounded to one straight run and would have to flatten this dogleg into treads through a wall.

**5. The other 55 sections are counted by name, not dropped.** The adapter declares what it left behind and the reader carries the declaration to the project panel. Not-lifted must never mean not-mentioned
column2: a user is entitled to know their file carries 47 lighting points this build does not draw, and not to find that out by noticing the ceiling is empty.

column1: **6. Plan.** Furniture footprints, the plates' edges and voids, and the stair's nosings and direction of travel. Three decisions each came from looking at the result rather than reasoning about it:

- **Furniture is an obstacle a room label must clear.** Left out first, reasoning that plans do print names over furniture — they do, over a rug, never over a kitchen island. ""Kitchen 35.3 m²"" came out struck through.
- **A room with nowhere clear keeps its name anyway.** Honouring the furniture strictly cost Guest bedroom, Study and office and Utility and laundry their labels
column2: the search now falls back.

column1: - **Label text is knocked out of what is behind it**, stroked in the paper colour before it is filled. That is what makes the fallback legible.

**7. Furniture is filled with the material the model states.** Put beside the package's own A101 — generated from this same model — the render had the right furniture in the right places and said nothing about what any of it is. `furnishingPrimitives` asserted outline-only and had a paragraph defending it
column2: that reasoning was wrong about the drawing it was protecting. A material the appearance names no colour for stays an outline rather than being given a colour the file never claimed.

column1: **8. 3D.** `plateSolids` cuts a plate along its hole edges into rectangles — `extrudePolygonMesh` caps with a triangle fan, so a floor drawn straight from the outline would have been solid across the courtyard and would have looked convincing. `stairFlightSolids` builds one solid per tread, each standing on the base: the underside of a stair over a landing is a place a person walks.
### Alignment faults found by measuring the running product
- **Every level shares one page.** The sheet was sized from the level on show, so each floor got its own — switching floors resized and moved the drawing, and the title and tools jumped 51px with it.
- **The docked rails are one column.** `TOOL_RAIL_DOCK_WIDTH_PX` was 48 against the mode rail's 56 — right edges 8px apart, icon centres 4.5px off a shared axis. Now 56/56.
- **Sheet chrome never sits flush to the edge** — its clamp bottomed out at 0.
- **The refraction lens escaped the control it decorates.** `.arq-view-kinds` had no positioning context, so the lens landed at x=85 over the project title with a distortion filter on it.
### The door hand, settled by evidence

`hand: 'start'` → `left` hinged the front door on the wrong jamb and swung it onto the street. Flipping *both* fields looked right and was also wrong: `plan-openings.ts` rotates `side` from the **closed leaf direction**, which depends on which jamb `hand` picked, so the two are not independent. Checked against A101, `start` is `right` and `side` keeps its polarity.
### Two checks that were reporting on code they had not run

- **`run-house-17-open-capability-check.mjs` built only when `dist/index.html` was missing.** It answered ""is there a build?"" where the only admissible question is ""is there a build of *this* code?"". It passed a change that adds 140 visible objects and screenshotted none of them. Every other capability check here already builds unconditionally, and `run-workspace-layout` records being bitten the same way.

- **Nothing ever opened the 3D tab.** The segments are `role=""tab""`, so an earlier `getByRole('button')` lookup matched nothing and passed silently — the model surface had been drawing walls and only walls for as long as the check existed. It now opens 3D and asserts colour variety as well as ink, because a walls-only model is nearly monochrome.
### The ""30 MB limit"" was never the cause

`preflightArqfsBytes` allows **8 GiB**, `MAX_ARCHIVE_TOTAL_BYTES` 1 GiB, `MAX_ENTRY_BYTES` 500 MiB — the 34.7 MB file was ~250× under the smallest gate. Opening is entirely client-side, so there is no upload to be too large for. The real cause was the silent degradation above, which is why compaction did not help: both files' `model.json` is byte-identical.
Writing an adapted model back into a `.arq`, and making Arq imitate the PDF generator's sheet furniture, label style or palette.
Not assessed: whether the 17.0 geometry is architecturally correct, and the structural, electrical, plumbing, HVAC and construction approval gates.
## What the file itself gets wrong

`validation/arq-house-17/FIXTURE_DEFECTS_17_0.md` records an audit of the fixture, for whoever generates it. The model is unusually clean — 706 unique ids, zero unresolved references, zero openings past their host wall, zero rooms whose stated area disagrees with their own polygon, zero furniture outside its assigned room, stair arithmetic exact — which is what makes the exceptions worth naming:
- **Two structural grids that disagree**, with nothing saying which is authoritative. The only outright contradiction in the model.
- **Four services points assigned to rooms they are not in**, one of them 11.4 metres out.
- **A 3.2 metre interior wall with no height, alignment, join intent or role.**
- **`side: ""configured""` on all 39 doors and windows** — a placeholder shaped like data.
- **No dimensions anywhere**, under any key, so no Arq drawing of this file can be dimensioned.
- **The courtyard tree is a prose sentence** while the 11 planters beside it are real objects Arq already draws.
- **~17 MB of the 34.7 MB is duplicate bytes** — 66 of 72 resources stored twice, the model stored three times, two different documentation PDFs both marked `portable-preview`.

`validation/arq-house-17/screenshots/` — ground, upper and 3D rendered from the real `house.arq` in headless Chromium, committed so the result can be looked at rather than trusted. Two confirmations fall out that this PR does not itself assert: the level list reports **31/25/12 walls**, matching the fixture's own `VALIDATION_REPORT_17_0.json` exactly, and the product's own area calculation puts the courtyard at **36.0 m² on ground and 36.0 m² void on upper**.

- `door-swing-matches-fixture.test.ts` asserts **where the leaf ends up**, not the enum values — an enum-only test would pass while the door swung through the front wall.

- `plateCells` is checked for area conservation and cell disjointness, not just ""it returned something"": a cell left standing over the courtyard is a floor where there is a six-metre drop, and it would look entirely convincing.
- **Full suite green: 350 files, 3845 tests, 0 failures.** ESLint, `tsc --noEmit` and Prettier clean.
- Capability checks: `native-open` ok, `workspace-layout` 8/8 viewports, `sheet-chrome` 3/3, `optical-glass` 4/4, and `check:house-17-open` passing with the file byte-identical.

## What the product does now that it did not

- **Semantic plan from canonical data.** The golden fixture's ground floor draws as a plan: 37 poché-filled walls, tinted and labelled rooms, and its doors and windows as real openings — piers, jambs, leaves, swing arcs, glazing. An opening is a hole, not a lid: the wall is drawn as the stretches that remain solid, so it cannot print solid over its own doors.
- **Opening-aware 3D.** The same canonical openings cut through the extruded model. One derivation feeds both surfaces, because two would let plan and model disagree about where an opening is.
- **Vector sheet export.** `Export sheet as PDF` at 1:100 on A1. Scale is honoured rather than fitted to page — a drawing issued at 1:100 must measure 1:100 under a rule.
- **Portable publication.** `Save a copy`, verified by a fresh independent reader before any bytes are handed over, with all twelve refusal reasons given distinct, truthful copy.
- **Condition-aware open.** A working copy whose last write never committed opens read-only and says so, instead of committing on top of a revision the project never reached.
- **Designed dark appearance and a bounded material layer,** under ADR-0031 and ADR-0032.

The V13 package explicitly rejects `Untitled project`, `demo fixture`, `Fixture wall N`, and hard-coded rectangular demo models. All are gone: the 5,000 synthetic tree rows, the hard-coded 4.20 × 3.60 room in plan, the 3D starting-room outline, the two invented tree nodes, and a Delete action that journalled a note instead of deleting.

`scripts/run-responsive-capture.mjs` captures the running product at each class in a real browser laid out at that size, with the pointer type that band really has, opening the golden fixture through the real dialog. Nothing is scaled, reused between sizes, or shown in a device frame.
| Viewport | Band the product resolved | Canvas | Fixture opens | Overflow |

Each asserts in-page: no `demo fixture` string, no `Fixture wall` string, no horizontal overflow. A 1366px iPad landing on `desktop` is an open threshold decision for the owner, recorded rather than silently moved.

Every canvas above is wider than an earlier revision of this table recorded, and none of it came from a layout change: the browser's default `body { margin: 8px }` had never been reset, so the shell was inset 8px on every side of every band.
Most were invisible to the test suite and only surfaced by driving the running application: no `font-family` anywhere (the product rendered in the browser's default serif)

column1: Three I caused and repaired in the same runs, each caught by a browser check rather than by tests or typecheck:
- Removing the 3D demo room left an empty scene with no bounding sphere → NaN radius → `fitBoundingSphere` threw during render and the 3D canvas never mounted.
- A *value* import from the `@arq/arqfs` barrel dragged `node:fs` into the browser bundle and failed the build.
- The capture harness waited for a string only the desktop panel renders, and nearly published ""the fixture did not open"" as a phone and iPad product failure.
### Correction pass: twelve more, found by reading the captures
Each verified against the running product after the fix. Full table and reasoning in the V13 ledger.

- **Room labels drawn through the walls and door swings on top of them.** The fit test compared bounding boxes, which is only right for a room that is a centred rectangle — and a label is drawn at the *centroid*. Worse, containment in a room's own ring cannot see an interior wall crossing a room whose boundary predates it (the fixture's ""Linen"" has exactly that), or a door swing, which sweeps into a room by design and belongs to no boundary at all. Walls and openings are now built before labels and handed over as clearance, and a label is offered the room's centre first and then positions further out rather than one position and nothing else.
- **The page inset 8px on every side of every band**, cutting sync state off the bottom of a 1024px window and taking 16px of width from a 430px phone.

- **The status strip reporting a cursor a touch device has not got**, and repeating save and sync from the bar directly above it. It keys on the pointer now, and the phone's separate tool chip — a third stacked strip above the dock — joins it.
- **An empty 38px context bar** across the bottom of the drawing, because ""there is an active tool"" was true on arrival with no actions to put in it.
- **The view identity pill printed over a room** wherever the drawing was fitted to fill.
- **The 3D ground plane swamping the building.** A fixed 30m square centred on the world origin, never re-placed

A single green chip tells a user their work is somewhere other than this device. It is not.

column1: PR-302,"Zeus 5: full prompt visibility, delegated-prompt lint, and the senior company role layer",closed,"[""E00""]",,https://github.com/ruddvz/Arq/pull/302,Closed without merge: compare patch/acceptance against successors before salvaging or retiring.,proposed title route,"## Problem

Zeus 5 routed every prompt but showed only its compact contract, so the operator never saw the actual instructions the executor works from, delegated prompts to subagents had no enforced shape, and there was no senior role layer (CEO/CTO/engineering leads) fronting the Zeus owner roles.

- The `UserPromptSubmit` hook now echoes, after the compact contract, the **full execution prompt** the contract compiles into: owner role, routed modules, method stack with effects, execution steps, check ladder, acceptance criteria, repair budget, handoff states, and always-on standing orders (including ""any prompt written for a subagent is shown in full before dispatch""). New CLI: `node scripts/zeus.mjs prompt --task ""...""` (`--with-contract`, `--format json`). `ZEUS_HOOK_PROMPT=0` reduces the echo to the compact contract alone.

- New `node scripts/zeus.mjs prompt-lint`: lints a delegated handoff prompt for the seven parts `/zeus-handoff` defines (role, context, task, acceptance, verification, critique, handoff), warns on missing non-goals, missing typed-evidence language, thin inlined context, and unmentioned authority gates. The generated execution prompt passes its own lint.

- New `company/` layer: fourteen senior roles (CEO, CTO, Chief of Staff, VP Engineering, Backend/Frontend/Geometry-BIM/AI/Security/QA leads, Product Manager, Design Lead, Marketing & Comms, Incident Commander) as context packs bound to `.zeus/role-registry.json` owner roles and the existing reviewer agents (`company/ROSTER.md`, `company/ZEUS-BRIDGE.md`). `node scripts/zeus.mjs roles --task ""...""` now prints the company face per role
column2: the new `/zeus-team` command runs one task through the whole chain autonomously. Patterns ported from the bookphysio CLEO system and adapted to Arq's contracts.

column1: - No change to classification, routing, tiers, budgets, guards, or the merge authority: roles and prompt visibility add transparency and a named owner, never authority. Engineering OS 5.0 still owns the gate and the Language System still owns wording.

column2: company roles are context packs, not `.claude/agents` entries.

column1: Not a UI change. Hook output sample (per actionable prompt): compact contract heading followed by `# Zeus 5 Execution Prompt` with the full instruction block.

All local, all green: `bash scripts/test-zeus-system.sh` (verify, hook tests incl. two new assertions for the execution-prompt echo and the `ZEUS_HOOK_PROMPT=0` opt-out, validation, classification, guard tests, architecture lint), `pnpm arq:language:verify`, `pnpm arq:language:audit:ci`, `pnpm check:secrets`, `pnpm check:workspace-registries`, prettier and eslint on changed scripts, and `zeus prompt | zeus prompt-lint` round-trip.
The hook now renders one extra markdown block per actionable prompt from the already-compiled contract
column2: compile stays in the microsecond range (precompiled matchers unchanged).

column1: None (internal tooling and markdown docs only).
None. No `.arq`, schema or persistence surface touched.
None. No dependencies added or changed
column2: new scripts use `node:fs` only.

column1: No new secret handling or network access. The delegated-prompt standing order plus `prompt-lint` reduce the risk of dispatching under-specified or unseen prompts
column2: the deterministic guards are untouched and still pinned by `zeus-guard-test.mjs` (23 cases green).
`ZEUS_HOOK_PROMPT=0` also disables the new hook output without a revert. New files (`company/`, `zeus-prompt*.mjs`, `/zeus-team`) are additive and safe to delete.

column1: PR-301,"Implement the ARQ CAD Pack 3.0 backlog: lifecycle, operations, units, references, constraints, inference",merged,"[""E00""]",,https://github.com/ruddvz/Arq/pull/301,Retain merged implementation/history
column2: a merge does not certify the whole product.,proposed title route,"## Problem

column1: The ARQ CAD System Implementation Pack 3.0 carries a 205-task backlog (`machine/backlog-v3.csv`), every row `state: proposed`. Much of P1–P3 was already merged at HEAD
column2: the phases that gate everything downstream were not implemented.

column1: Forty commits across P1–P13. **`docs/product/V3-IMPLEMENTATION-TRACEABILITY.csv` maps all 205 tasks** to where each was addressed or why it was not — read that first, it is the only way to check this PR's claims task by task.
| Owner-authority (P0 checks, P14 release, workflow pinning, build provenance) | 28 |
| Implemented differently (V3-032, V3-035, V3-039, V3-142, V3-143, V3-148) | 6 |
| Blocked for want of evidence (V3-107, V3-108, V3-117) | 3 |

The record is generated and every row verified: each names an evidence path and a symbol that must appear in it, and the generator fails rather than writing a claim the repository cannot support. It failed once while being written — a job in `security.yml` rather than `ci.yml`.

The flow reached `published` directly from `publishing` on a bare event, while its own copy told the user *""The published file was reopened and checked""*. Nothing performed that check — the reassurance was the fabricated part. `publishProjectFile` reopens published bytes through a reader sharing no page cache, statement cache or transaction with the writer, and requires that reader's own findings to match on identity, revision and semantic hash. A dropped-entry test proves the point: SQLite still considers that file sound.

`RecoveryPlan.autoApply` is the literal type `false`, so no caller can build a plan that authorises its own application. A journal built on a revision *newer* than the working copy is refused whole, since replaying the matching subset would commit a partial history.

**Publication is now reachable from the browser.** It runs as a Worker command, because `VACUUM INTO` writes through the VFS and only the Worker holds the `opfs-sahpool` utility that can reopen the result as an independent connection — a main thread handed the bytes and asked to verify them would be checking a copy of a copy, which is the property publication depends on, broken. The bytes and the verdict travel on one response, so no caller can hand a file to a user without the receipt saying it was checked
column2: a verified publication that returns no bytes is reported as a refusal, because a success with no file is the one outcome that must not be called success. `NativeProjectSession.publish` queues behind in-flight saves rather than racing them into a `working-copy-not-settled` refusal.

column1: One commit path: refuse read-only, reject a stale base revision, check preconditions against current state, apply, validate the *candidate*, commit in one transaction, read the revision back rather than incrementing locally. Every rejection returns the caller's original state and revision, asserted across all six rejection paths.

The spike measures rather than argues, and **contradicts the pack's own reasoning**: `bigint` is 13.6× slower, while integer micrometres in a `number` are about twice as fast as float64. The assumed cost of the decision is not a cost. What it confirms is why it matters — float64 fails route-independent equality (300mm reached two ways are different floats), which is what makes a semantic hash unusable as proof a migration preserved meaning. **Still Proposed**: representation only.

A slab's `datumFace` is required — a 200mm floor whose *top* sits at level datum and one whose *bottom* does occupy different space. A stair stores riser *count*, since the levels fix the total rise, and its comfort limits are `PROVISIONAL` because real limits come from a jurisdiction's code profile. A material carries every property with its provenance. A schedule stores the question and never the answer.
Typing a room name and pressing `W` no longer fires the wall tool
column2: the rule is total by default, because every candidate for a punch-through list already means something inside a text field. Splitting a wall no longer drops its doors — reassigned deterministically, or the split is blocked and the straddling opening named. Selection works without a pointer, and hidden nodes stay selectable, because a hidden object cannot be clicked at all.

column1: float32 resolves ~60mm at 1000km, so a georeferenced site snaps to a grid coarser than its own walls — origin rebasing removes AC3-070's jitter and mis-picking, tested against `Math.fround` rather than a model of the loss. Invalidation is driven by *effect*, not operation type, so a rename no longer re-meshes a building. Derived geometry declares itself underivable-from: `meshIsMeasurable` and `meshEditIsPersistable` return false unconditionally. Hiding and clipping are view properties — `visibleForSchedule` and `sectionBoxAffectsQuantities` say so in code, because a schedule agreeing with the drawing would under-order. A sheet crop is model-space, so rescaling shrinks the drawing rather than growing a west wing
column2: annotation prints at 2.5mm at every scale. A schedule that overflows reports a count and the sheets it needs. PDF generation moved off the main thread with acknowledged cancellation, and exported bytes are read back by an independent reader that measures the printed scale rather than trusting a title block.

column1: `disabled` removes a control from the tab order, so a keyboard user never learns why it cannot be used
column2: `aria-disabled` keeps it reachable and the resulting obligation is returned alongside the attributes. Live regions coalesce per region and never delay an assertive message. Long names truncate in the middle, because ""…- Planning - REV C"" and ""REV D"" differ at the end. `dialogFits` checks the smallest viewport and 200% text *together*, which is the case that actually breaks. Pencil ownership survives the palm lifting after the stylus — the naive rule ends the stroke at the user's wrist. `NON_COLOUR_STATE_CUES` pins that no state is carried by colour alone, which forced colours would erase.

column1: Everything above introduced states, refusals and reports with no entry in the governed vocabulary, so the Language System could not check any of them. Three new state machines (`view-visibility`, `section-box`, `import-units`), a `reversed` proposal state, eleven message IDs, thirteen prohibited upgrades (hidden→removed, clipped→deleted, quarantined→imported, written→published, approved→applied), three fidelity terms, and announcement profiles matching what `live-region-queue` enforces. A fourth read-only cause, `another-window-is-editing`, joins them: telling someone their file is too new when they simply have it open in another tab is a wrong answer to the only question they are asking. The full ladder passes.

A proposal is a request. The grant is a separate argument to `evaluateProposal`, never a field on the proposal, so no wording a model produces can widen it — three injection tests come at it from different angles. Extensions declare a closed capability set, and the host boundary is a closed union of plain serialisable messages with no variant able to carry a handle. An import whose units are unknown is refused rather than guessed. Unsupported entities are quarantined with their payload. A compressed source is bounded by ratio *while it decompresses*. Telemetry gains the allowlist half a denylist cannot provide.
### Auditing the traceability record, and what it found (P1–P3, P7)

`pre-existing` was the disposition the record itself flagged as worth reading sceptically: it meant ""the repository already had the module the task names"", not ""the task is finished"". Reading all 65 of those rows rather than trusting that caveat moved thirteen rows and found **eight real defects**. The recurring shape was a module that exists, is correct, and is well tested — wired to nothing that needed it.

- **V3-030, the single-writer lock ADR-0024 specifies, was never acquired.** `acquireSingleWriterLock` had no caller outside its own tests, so `readOnly` came only from the file's writer-version floor. Two windows could open one project writable, each believing it was the writer. The suite was green throughout, because a lock nobody takes breaks no test. The lease is now taken before the Worker is constructed — a contended project is not first imported into a working copy another context holds — and released when the session closes or the open fails.

- **V3-038, open never checked a file's own digests.** A `.arq` carries `checksums.json` recording what every entry should hash to. `verifyArqfsEntryDigests` had exactly one caller: publication. So a file this build had just written was verified, and a file from anywhere else was adopted on trust — a `model.json` edited to remain valid JSON would decode into whatever it now said and become the project. Open refuses it now, before the archive is parsed.

- **V3-021, neither Worker validated its incoming message.** `handleArqfsWorkerRequest`'s switch is exhaustive over the union, so an unrecognised `type` fell through and returned `undefined`, which the Worker posted — the caller waited out a full timeout for a request refused on arrival, contradicting that function's own documented contract.

- **V3-090, the snap sources and the layer that ranks them had no path between them.** `rankCandidates` took a `SnapResult[]` and nothing built one. `inference-engine.ts` names the gap in its own doc comment and then supplies the ranking half only.

column2: a merge does not certify the whole product.,proposed title route,"Implements the Implementation Pack 3.0's P5 (portable publication) and closes a real, previously-unfixed async race, reconciled against the real repository rather than the revision the pack observed.

column1: **This PR's scope changed twice while it was open.** It began as an independent implementation of the native open path
column2: PR-294 merged the same objective mid-flight, so `6c29e70` reconciles onto the merged implementation and drops this branch's duplicates, keeping only what the merged path didn't have (a working-copy integrity check). Everything from `4abed44` onward is new: publication.

column1: Opening is not saving"" was `STATUS.md`'s own honest boundary. There was no way to turn an open project's working copy into a portable `.arq` file, and the pack's own rule for what counts as a publication is strict: nothing may be called published until a completely independent reader has reopened the bytes and confirmed they mean the same thing as the source.

Building the export side of the Worker protocol surfaced a real, already-shipped defect: `importDatabase`'s Worker implementation called `poolUtil.importDb(...)` — which returns a Promise — without awaiting it, then opened a fresh connection over the target file on the very next line. Nothing had caught it because every existing capability check's payload was small and fast enough for the race to usually lose.

**Worker protocol** (`4abed44`): `exportDatabase` switches the connection out of WAL mode with `journal_mode=DELETE` (a checkpoint alone is insufficient — it merges pending frames but leaves the header still declaring WAL, caught by an adversarial test that fed checkpointed-but-not-mode-switched bytes back through the byte-level preflight) and returns the working copy's bytes. `computeSemanticHash` exposes the existing `computeProjectSemanticHash` over the protocol. `handleArqfsWorkerRequest` is now properly `async`, which is what let the import race be fixed.

**The publish pipeline** (`9e529bb`): `NativeProjectSession.prepareForPublication` drains every in-flight write through the *same* queue `save` uses — queued as a step in that chain, not a spectator of it, so a `save` issued after publish starts cannot race the export — then checkpoints and exports. `publishNativeProject` reopens those bytes through `openNativeProject` on a Worker the *caller* constructs fresh (never derived from the source session, since a fresh reader that shared state with the writer wouldn't prove anything), compares project id, revision (`#operations.length`, not the caller-overridable `journalSequence`) and semantic hash, and closes the verification session regardless of outcome.

**Wired into the product** (`dcf9d25`): ""Publish project…"" in the command palette and phone menu, real disabled reasons, real outcome reported through the same command-feedback region undo/redo already use.

Canvas edits still don't reach `NativeProjectSession.save` — nothing in `apps/web` calls it — so publish today republishes exactly what was opened, not live edits. `STATUS.md` and the register say this plainly rather than implying more. No browser/OPFS capability check for publish exists yet (unlike `benchmark:file-open` for opening)
column2: that and the numerics/tolerance foundation (P8) are next. No GitHub, Vercel, branch, release or production state touched.

column1: This branch originally added a `vercel.json` that deployed the marketing site only. **PR #294 merged to base first with a materially more complete deployment**, and this PR is now the merge of that plus the one property it lacked.

#294 ships one artifact holding both public surfaces — marketing at `/`, the browser editor at `/app/` — with security headers, a three-tier cache split keyed on whether the filename carries a content hash, `/Arq/*` compatibility redirects, and `scripts/verify-vercel-routes.mjs` checking the deployed origin rather than the build. That is a strict superset of what this branch proposed.
So the `vercel.json` conflict is resolved **in favour of theirs, wholesale**, and `scripts/vercel-build.sh` is deleted.
## The one property that did not survive the swap

A hosted build clones a *branch*, not a commit. Between the moment a release is approved at some revision and the moment Vercel checks out, the branch can move — and nothing downstream notices, because the deployment reaches READY either way and the revision recorded in the proof comes from the same drifted checkout, so it agrees with itself and confirms nothing.

`scripts/build-vercel.mjs` **recorded** `sourceCommit` without ever **comparing** it to anything. It now compares against `EXPECTED_SOURCE_SHA`, before any build step runs, and fails on mismatch — the same binding `.github/workflows/deploy-pages.yml` already gets from `scripts/write-deployment-provenance.mjs`, so both hosts hold the published artifact to one rule rather than two.

An unset variable stays a pass, on purpose. A preview builds whatever its branch points at, so there is no independent expectation to check it against and requiring one would only produce a check that always passes. Set it on production
column2: leave it unset on previews.

column1: | `EXPECTED_SOURCE_SHA` set to a different revision | build fails before any build step runs | ✅ exit 1, no build step reached |
| `EXPECTED_SOURCE_SHA` set to the checked-out revision | build proceeds to the gates | ✅ reached `arq:language:verify` |

The outcome is recorded as well as enforced: `deployment-source.json` and the `vercelDeployment` block in the site proof both carry `expectedCommit` and `sourcePinned`, so a reader of the deployed artifact can tell an approved release from a preview that was free to build whatever it found.

column1: ADR-0028 is now Accepted, so the lifecycle it governs can be built. This is the state machine half.

The existing reducer stopped at `native-opening`, which means only *""the bytes passed preflight""*. Everything after — staging a copy, verifying migration on that copy, opening the Worker, hydrating, activating — had **no representation at all**. Any surface wanting to know whether a project was open had to decide for itself, from a state that did not answer the question.
**Extended, not replaced.** A second state machine for the same flow would be two sources of truth for one question, and they would drift.

Failure is **one kind with an exhaustive reason**, not a dozen near-identical kinds. Every failure leaves the flow in the same shape — nothing open, previous project untouched, a specific cause to show — and splitting that would duplicate the structure and let the cases drift. The reason is a closed union, so a new cause cannot arrive as a string nobody wrote copy for.
## Three invariants enforced in code, not by convention

**1. No false open.** `isProjectOpen` is true *only* in `workspace-active` — not `worker-open` (the Worker holds the file but no semantic state exists yet), not `hydrating` (partway through). A test asserts every earlier state answers false:
✓ reports no state before workspace-active as open

**2. Read-only survives to the end.** `writable` is decided once at Worker open and carried on the state. My first attempt kept it in a module-level `Map` — hidden mutable state inside a pure reducer. Carrying it on the state removes that, and makes a read-only file provably still read-only when the workspace activates.
**3. Last known good rides on the failure states.** A failed open, quarantine, cancellation and close all keep it, so a failure cannot silently replace the project the user already had.

Transitions name both source state and event, so an out-of-order event is ignored rather than skipping a stage. Skipping is the dangerous direction — it is how a project reaches active without being hydrated.
| `cancel` in an active workspace | ignored — cannot invent an undo that never happened |

Every new state goes through `describeFileFlowState`, whose exhaustive switch made the compiler list exactly which states were missing. **No new copy says ""open"" except `workspace-active`.** Staging and migration both say the original file is not changed. Recovery says the changes are on this device and not in the project file yet.
| language ladder incl. state-language coverage | pass |
| Engineering OS policy, fixtures, context | pass |
| architecture lint, security lint, secret scan | pass |
`apps/web/src/file-handling` is a governed source set, so the language context was refreshed in the same change — the freshness gate caught it before CI did.

**This is the state machine only.** It is not wired to the Worker yet, so no surface claims a project can be opened and STATUS.md is unchanged on that point. Wiring, the browser evidence matrix, and the UI states follow in their own changes.
Ordinary revert. No schema, migration, dependency or lockfile change. Existing states and transitions are untouched, so the current file-open behaviour is unaffected.

column1: It opened as a second implementation of native `.arq` open, built on a memory-resident read-only connection while ADR-0028 was still Proposed. While it was open, #294 landed the same feature on the base branch from a different architecture — an OPFS working copy under the now-Accepted ADR-0030.

Two open pipelines in one app is not a merge result worth having, so the base's is the one that survives. This PR is reduced to what #294 does not already have, plus two defects found while integrating.

**Deleted from this branch**, because #294 covers them: the memory-resident pipeline (`native-open-pipeline`, `open-native-project`, `active-project`, `arqfs-worker-transport`, `arqfs-selected-bytes-db`) and this branch's additions to the arqfs Worker protocol, handler, client and entry. The base's versions are taken wholesale, including its read gating and its `-wal` sidecar refusal.

`decodeNativeProjectModel` required a root `projectName`. The real Arq model has none — it carries a project summary with its own id, name, units and revision, plus levels, wall types, rooms and views. So the shipped product could open the files it had written and refused the reference fixture outright:

It now falls back to `@arq/project-loading` when the flat shape is absent, and reports which shape arrived rather than flattening both. A project carrying a reference document gets a project browser: its levels with real per-level wall and room counts, its own model tree, an inspector reading through real wall types, level switching and close.
## Two defects the browser check found

**Choosing the open project reported that it could not be opened.** The working copy is content-addressed, so the same bytes name the same OPFS file and the same dedicated Worker file. Adoption closes the previous session only after the new open succeeds — correct, because a failed open must leave the previous project untouched — so the second Worker tried to take a working copy the live one still held. The product said ""could not be opened"" about a project sitting on screen.

`openNativeProject` now compares the content-addressed id against the working copy the workspace holds, before any Worker is constructed, and answers `already-open`. Both adoption-boundary guarantees survive. The comparison is keyed off a working-copy id tracked for every open, not off the project browser's model — that only exists for files carrying a reference document, and keying it there would have left the flat shape this build writes still able to hit it.

**Every level was drawn at once.** The snapshot carries all 79 walls across three levels and the plan drew all of them, so switching level changed nothing: the ground and upper floors had byte-identical pixel checksums because the upper floor was already on top. The surfaces are now fed the level on show. The project's own wall ids are carried through unchanged, because they are what the model tree selects by and what 3D highlights by.
Three things this branch used to say are no longer true and are not carried forward.
- The panel said **""Read-only.""** The base's working copy is writable. It now says ""Working copy."" and where a change actually lands: nothing is written back to the `.arq` file the reader chose.

- `benchmark:native-open` asserted the **wall tool is disabled**. It should not be — the project has somewhere to put a wall. The check now asserts the shell never claims ""Saved locally"", which is the claim that would genuinely be false.
- `workersAfterThreeOpens === 1` was worded as proving **each replacement terminates the one before**. It never did

column1: PR 01 of the blocker-closure programme. Every later workstream depends on decisions that were recorded as Proposed and on identifiers that nothing enforced. This establishes that base and **deliberately implements no project-open code**.

- **ADR-0028 Proposed → Accepted** (D-024). SQLite in an ARQ-owned dedicated Worker over OPFS owns the canonical local working project. IndexedDB is bounded to recovery bridging, source provenance, last-known-good pointers, resumable publication metadata, device preferences and replaceable derived caches during migration. **A journal append is not a portable save.**

- **ADR-0029 adopts `main`** as the stable integration and production branch (D-025), through a reversible migration that keeps the current branch undeleted through a rollback window. **The migration is not performed here.**
Acceptance unblocks the open pipeline. It does not implement it, and STATUS.md still says so.
Those decisions are worth exactly as much as the ids that carry them, and nothing checked them.

`scripts/verify-decision-ids.mjs` runs in two modes. Tree mode is the obvious one. **Base mode is the one that matters:** draft PR #280 adds a second `ADR-0027` and redefines `D-024`, and it is *internally consistent on its own branch* — so a tree-only check passes it. Only comparing against the base shows both ids were taken by work that merged first.
The self-test asserts that asymmetry on a real git history:
PASS the collision branch passes a tree-only check, which is why it was missed
PASS the collision branch fails the base comparison
PASS the base comparison names the reused ADR file id
PASS the base comparison names the redefined decision
**Two design corrections, both found by the check rejecting legitimate work and both pinned as regression tests:**
1. Exact text equality rejected accepting D-024 in place, because its text began with the word ""Proposed"". A check that blocks ordinary governance gets switched off.
2. Jaccard similarity was tried next and was also wrong — it scores *adding detail* as low as *replacing* the decision. The rule now uses an overlap coefficient.

`engines.node` was `"">=20""` with no upper bound — a claim that every future Node major works, while every workflow pins 20. Now `"">=20 <23""`, the range actually exercised. `scripts/verify-toolchain-policy.mjs` fails if a workflow steps outside it or overrides the pnpm pin. The unbounded range is what the check caught first.
A hosted build clones a *branch*, so it can move between approval and checkout. The footer revision comes from the same drifted checkout, agrees with itself, and confirms nothing.

The expected SHA now arrives from the event rather than the working tree, a mismatch **fails the Pages job before upload**, and the artifact carries a provenance record with both SHAs, toolchain, per-route and per-file hashes.
| expected SHA differs | **fail**, names both SHAs |
Provenance is written even on failure, because a blocked release is exactly when the record is needed.
The GitHub API returns `visibility: public`, `private: false`, `allow_forking: true`, `license: NOASSERTION`, while `LICENSE` says ""proprietary and confidential"".

The proprietary grant is **untouched** — that is the owner's decision with legal advice. ""Confidential"" is a claim about who can read the repository, and it is contradicted by the repository being publicly readable and forkable by anyone. Both resolutions and their consequences are recorded in `LICENSE-DECISION-REQUIRED.md` for the owner to choose. No public surface states a licence position.

`engineering/36_REQUIRED_CHECK_ROLLOUT.md` records what must hold before the gate becomes required — including that its own `protected_l4_approval` currently resolves to a **deferred environment gate rather than an approval anybody granted**, and that one green run is not a rollout criterion.

column1: Reconciled from the ARQ Native Project Open and Vercel Implementation Pack v2.0 (SHA-256 `0a62e551…`, checksum verified) against this repository. The pack is evidence, not authority — live implementation and accepted ADRs outrank it (`.zeus/INVARIANTS.md`), and each proposal was checked for an existing equivalent, ADR conflict, and whether it would create a second source of truth.
Three defects confirmed by reading the live code rather than trusting the pack:

1. **`arqfs-worker-handler.ts` gated writes but not reads.** `getArchiveEntry` and `listArchiveEntryPaths` called straight through to the store. A Worker holding an open driver would hand back project bytes for a file it had never opened — and for a file whose open it had explicitly *rejected*, since rejection leaves the driver connected and records a verdict those paths never read.

2. **A database missing its `-wal` sidecar was presented as openable.** SQLite opens it without error and serves the last checkpoint, so the user sees an apparently healthy project silently missing their most recent saved work. The product showed a caution next to it.

3. **`ArqfsWorkerRequestInput` was `Omit`.** `keyof` a union is only the keys common to all members, so it collapsed to `{ type }` and discarded `path` and `entries` — every parameterized Worker request was untypeable.
Verified absent from the repository at the fork point: `apps/web/src/project/`, `packages/arqfs/src/arqfs-source-completeness.ts`, `vercel.json`.

Choosing a `.arq` file now opens it. The byte-level checks run first and refuse before anything is constructed — a refusal must not cost an OPFS working copy — then the bytes are imported into a working copy via a new `importDatabase` Worker command (`opfs-sahpool` keeps databases in opaque pool files, so this has to go through `poolUtil.importDb` inside the Worker entry), opened through sqlite-wasm, decoded, and adopted into the workspace.

Every failure past Worker construction releases it. A leaked Worker holds the OPFS write lock on its working copy and makes that project unopenable for the rest of the session, so that is the property the tests assert on each rejection — not just the returned code.
Adoption is the caller's, never the panel's: the workspace replaces its project only once a candidate is fully decoded, so a rejected or cancelled file leaves whatever was already open untouched.

Nothing checkpoints edits back to the `.arq` file. The workspace reports the project as open and not saved, because saying `saved` would claim durability this build has not earned. Copy-on-write migration stays unreachable for the same reason, and `canMigrate` is treated as **read-only** rather than as permission to write (ADR-0030).

Reviewing the packages this one has to trust turned up defects in already-shipped code. Each was reproduced against the source before being touched, and each fix is proven by running the real tooling rather than by inspection.

**File integrity.** The `.arq` semantic hash concatenated path and content without length framing, so two different projects could hash identically - proven with a runnable collision before the fix, and the regression test proven non-vacuous by showing v1 collides where v2 does not. The arqfs worker asked `openArqfs` whether it could write and then ignored the answer, so a file this build had just declared itself unqualified to write could be mutated by the next message. The defensive open policy had no non-test caller, so `PRAGMA foreign_keys` stayed off in the real browser runtime and every `REFERENCES` the schema declares was inert. The single-writer lock used one global name, so opening project A blocked project B, and discarded the request's own rejection, so a refusal hung for ever instead of degrading. Byte preflight read the write-ahead-log header and returned it, but nothing drew the conclusion: SQLite opened without a `-wal` sidecar returns the database as of its last checkpoint rather than failing, so a picked `project.arq` could show a compatible, healthy project missing the user's newest work. A failed copy-on-write migration deleted the corrupt copy - the only evidence of a bug that corrupts projects during upgrade - and can now quarantine it instead.

**Privacy.** `redactSensitiveFields` matched exact camelCase only, so `project_name` passed through untouched, and declined to recurse into arrays, so `{ walls: [{ geometry: ... }] }` leaked entirely - a test asserted that leak as intended behaviour. Both closed.

**Accessibility.** The status bar carried `role=""status"" aria-live=""polite""` on its own `<footer>`, so every child announced itself on change including the cursor position, which changes on every pointer move. A polite region queues rather than interrupts, so a screen reader would read coordinates for ever and reach nothing else.

**Gate integrity.** The scripts that produce and check the gate's evidence classified as `unknown_runtime_surface`, so editing the wasm parity checker never selected `wasm_parity` - the check could be weakened in the change it was meant to measure. `wasm_parity` and `worker_core` both read a build artifact no workflow built, so both failed at ""pkg does not exist"" for every change that selected them, measuring the runner rather than the diff. `verify-workflow-templates.mjs` read reference templates this repository correctly never installed, threw `ENOENT` on every invocation and was wired to nothing. Six passing capability checks had no catalog id, so the gate could not select the single-writer lock check when the single-writer lock changed. `packages/mcp-server` itself - the AI trust boundary - had no change-map rule at all.

**Privacy transport.** `DRIFT-PRIVACY-TRANSPORT-ABSOLUTE` blocked the claim `no-network-data-transfer` at high severity for want of an instrument. `benchmark:network-observation` now records every request the real bundle attempts in headless Chromium while a wall is drawn, the 3D view opened and the file panel used, and fails if any leaves the origin that served it. It records rather than blocks, because blocking outbound traffic and observing none measures the harness

column1: This is the substance of the change.

- Every bridge method takes a `GrantContext` first: subject, tenant, client, scopes, exact projects, expiry, revocation, checked on every call. An unwired application gets a server where every tool answers ""nothing is shared with this connection"".
- A project outside the grant and one that does not exist give the same error, so one grant cannot enumerate an operator's other projects.
- Commit lives on `ArqOperatorSurface`, an object the server is never constructed with. The guarantee is scope, not a flag.

- Provenance is derived from the `initialize` handshake and the server clock. `rightsStatus: ""user_attests_permitted""` is not in the input vocabulary - software does not attest to a person's reuse rights.
- Reference URIs are parsed: no credentials, no IP literals, no reserved namespaces, no non-default ports, ASCII only. Nothing is ever fetched.
- The audit trail stores a request fingerprint and never request content, so it can prove what happened without becoming a second copy of every plan.
- The loopback HTTP endpoint requires a pairing token compared in constant time, refuses `localhost` (whose resolution can be redirected), and refuses every request when unpaired.
- `check-secrets.mjs` had no tests, so a regex broken by an edit would have reported a clean tree for ever. Its patterns are now pinned by `check-secrets-test.mjs`, which runs before the scan in CI.

column2: a merge does not certify the whole product.,proposed title route,"Upgrades the Arq operating system from Zeus 4.0 to 5.0. The uploaded `ZEUS_ARQ_OPERATOR_OS_2.0` package was used as reference material and critiqued, not installed as an overlay.

column1: Zeus 4 was fast and deterministic where it counted, but three things were wrong, and all three are reproducible on the Zeus 4 code:
**1. Trigger matching was a bare substring test.**
| `rename a variable in the parser guide` | `ui-visual` | ""ui"" inside ""g**ui**de"" |

**2. Mode came from keyword presence, not the speech act.** `explain how the build works` classified as `implement` because it contains ""build"". Worse, the delivery stop was raised unconditionally whenever ""deploy"", ""production"" or ""ship"" appeared anywhere, so `explain the release process` compiled a contract whose stop was `production-verified`. A question about releasing was gated as a production deployment.

**3. Risk was the only gating axis.** A low-risk edit to `packages/arqfs` and a low-risk edit to a README were treated identically. Risk says how likely a change is to be wrong. It says nothing about how far a wrong version reaches or what undoing it costs.

Separately, `scripts/test-zeus-system.sh` could not pass on the base branch: the four lint fixture directories it depends on (`quality/architecture-clean|bad`, `quality/fixtures/security-clean|bad`) were never committed.

**Routing.** Task and trigger are normalised the same way and matched on token and phrase boundaries with a bounded inflection suffix, so ""walls"" matches ""wall"" and ""wallpaper"" does not. Negative phrases added: ""unit test"" no longer routes geometry through ""unit"".

**Modes.** Read from clause openings. `answer` and `plan` modes cannot escalate the delivery stop, inherit the topic's risk, or buy a deep budget. Incidents are detected as a shared surface plus a failure word, so ""the ci is failing on main"" is caught where the fixed phrase ""ci failing"" was not.

**Two new axes.** Blast radius (`local`, `package`, `product`, `persistent`, `public`, `production`) and reversibility (`reversible`, `compensable`, `irreversible`), in `.zeus/blast-radius.json`. Derived from task language and, in `zeus impact`, from real changed paths, worst of the two winning. Either can raise a tier and add acceptance criteria
column2: neither can lower anything. Persistent radius adds original-preserved, copy-on-write and recovery evidence
column3: irreversible adds an operator confirmation step.

column1: Building this surfaced an over-escalation defect of my own: a module matching on one weak token dragged `rename a variable in the parser guide` into a deep public lane. Weak matches now contribute a capped radius, and that case classifies as package/fast.

**Method selection.** New. `.zeus/method-registry.json` holds 98 retained methods (94 distinct behaviours, 4 aliases) with scopes, so selection is deterministic and scope-gated: a marketing method is never proposed for a geometry defect. `zeus method` prints the stack with the reason for each entry.

column2: Zeus 5 grades each claim (`verified`, `partially-verified`, `inferred`, `assumed`, `blocked`, `not-inspected`, `failed`). Only `verified` is green and it requires a command and exit code. A cached entry for a protected gate is downgraded automatically. `zeus evidence report` exits non-zero otherwise.

column1: **One invariant register.** `.zeus/INVARIANTS.md`, 85 invariants in 13 sections, replacing copies that had drifted between the kernel and the modules. Modules apply it, reviewer agents verify against it, neither restates it.
**Independent reviewers.** Six domain reviewer subagents plus an orchestrator under `.claude/agents/`, each bound to the invariant sections it verifies and named by the compiled contract.

**Self-validation.** `zeus validate` cross-checks manifests, registries, skills, agents, hooks and schemas against each other. It fails if the Arq language guardian is ever removed from the hook chain, or if a Zeus skill stops pointing at a `.zeus/` source.
### Deliberately not adopted from the reference package

- Its `.claude/rules/` and `docs/operator-source/` trees duplicated `.zeus/modules/`, `docs/adr/` and `STATUS.md`. Installing them would have created a second source of truth for the same invariants. Content folded into `.zeus/INVARIANTS.md` instead.

- Its blocking write-time language guard duplicated the Arq Language System 4.1 (em dashes, hype, prohibited claims, interoperability overclaims) using path heuristics instead of real scope resolution, and blocked at write time where this repository deliberately warns at write and blocks in CI. Reduced to the product-safety absolutes the Language System does not carry, made warn-only, and scoped to files outside the guardian's reach so the two never double-report.
- Its 38 granular skills were kept but rewritten as thin routers into `.zeus/`, so a skill cannot drift from the module it describes.

- Its guards matched destructive patterns against the whole serialised tool payload, which blocks writing documentation that quotes a rejected pattern. Rewritten to match commands against commands and paths against paths.
- No change to Engineering OS 5.0, which remains the merge authority, or to the Arq Language System 4.1, which remains the language authority.
- No product code touched. This is operating-system and tooling only.
- `scripts/zeus-architecture-lint.mjs` still cannot tell a sentence stating a prohibition from one breaching it. Documented as a known limitation in the clean fixture rather than fixed here.
Not applicable. No user-facing surface changes.
- `scripts/zeus-classification-test.mjs`, 14 cases over `quality/fixtures/zeus-classification-cases.json`. Every routing and mode defect above is pinned, plus the new axes and scope gating.

- `scripts/zeus-guard-test.mjs`, 13 cases over `quality/fixtures/zeus-guard-cases.json`, pinning both sides of the guard: what must be blocked, and what must not (documenting a rejected pattern, editing an ArqScript `.arq` source, editing the env template, `grep process.env`).
- Evidence-ledger assertion in the system test: a run containing a `not-inspected` claim must not grade green.
- The four missing lint fixture directories, so `scripts/test-zeus-system.sh` passes end to end for the first time.

### CI corrections after the first push
Three checks failed on the first commit and were fixed in `fb91e6d`:

- **`preflight`**: the generated engineering context was stale. This change moves files inside the context's hashed source set, so it had to be rebuilt in the same commit, the same rule the Language System applies to its own context.
- **`engineering-gate`**: a cascade, not a separate defect. It downloads the selected-evidence artifact that `preflight` never produced.

- **`lint-and-typecheck`**: `format:check` failed on the three hook files and one skill. My first local run resolved Prettier through `npx` before `node_modules` existed, so it reported a different file set than the pinned version. Re-run with the pinned Prettier and fixed.
